title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Look It Up, Then Answer
summary: Ground a language model in your own documents: chunk them with overlap, embed and index the chunks, retrieve the closest ones by cosine similarity, and inject them into the prompt with citations and a strict context budget.
takeaways: RAG lets the model read the answer from retrieved text instead of recalling it, which gives fresher facts and citable sources.
Chunk with overlap so boundary sentences survive. The step is size − overlap, exactly.
Rank by cosine similarity, not raw dot product, and break ties deterministically.
Inject chunks in rank order with numbered citations, and count every character, newlines included, against the budget.

steps.label: Chunk
steps.detail: Split each document into overlapping windows of words.

steps.label: Embed + index
steps.detail: Turn every chunk into a unit vector and store it with its source.

steps.label: Retrieve
steps.detail: Embed the question and take the top-k chunks by cosine similarity.

steps.label: Inject
steps.detail: Add the chunks to the prompt as [n] (source) text until the budget is full.

steps.label: Generate
steps.detail: The LLM answers from the context and cites the [n] markers.

terms.definition: Conditioning a generator on passages retrieved from an external corpus at query time.
The number of words consecutive chunks share, so text that spans a boundary stays intact in at least one chunk.
Mapping tokens to vector indices with a hash function, so no vocabulary has to be stored.
q·d / (‖q‖‖d‖): the angle between two vectors, independent of their lengths.
The maximum amount of retrieved text allowed in the prompt, in characters or tokens.
